unit.title: In the Classroom: En el Salón de Clases

lesson.title: Saquen el Cuaderno: Classroom Commands You Act Out
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you learned the names of seven classroom objects. Today you learn what happens when a teacher tells the whole class to do something — the short command phrases you hear over and over in a Spanish classroom, and how to show you understand them without saying a word.

A command is a phrase that tells someone to do something right now: 'Line up.' 'Sit down.' A Spanish teacher talking to the whole class uses phrases like these:

saquen el cuaderno — take out your notebook
escuchen — listen
levanten la mano — raise your hand

Learn these as whole phrases, the way you already know that 'line up' means one thing even though it is two words. You are not learning yet how to build a command yourself or change it for one person versus a group — that comes later in the year. For now your only job is to hear one of these and know what to do.

Here are more class commands built from this week's words. The first word is the action; the rest is one of yesterday's objects:

saquen el bolígrafo — take out your pen
guarden la regla — put away your ruler
miren la pizarra — look at the board
abran el cuaderno — open your notebook
cierren el cuaderno — close your notebook

You do not have to memorize every action word perfectly yet. Listen for the object you already know — cuaderno, bolígrafo, regla, pizarra — and watch what your classmates do.

This is a Total Physical Response game: you prove you understand by moving, not by talking. Ask a parent or teacher to call these out in a mixed-up order while you act each one:

escuchen — cup a hand behind your ear
levanten la mano — raise your hand
saquen el cuaderno — mime pulling out a notebook
miren la pizarra — turn and look at the wall or board
guarden el bolígrafo — mime putting a pen away

Speed up little by little. If you do the wrong action, the caller just repeats the phrase slowly and you try again — no points lost.

You can now follow the everyday commands of a Spanish classroom — listen, raise your hand, take out your notebook, look at the board. Tomorrow you play a memory game: a tray of supplies, a ten-second look, then it is covered and you name everything that was there.

items.sentence: The teacher wants the class silent for a story. She calls out: '___.'
You know the answer and want to be called on. You '___ la mano.'
It is time to write. The teacher says: '___ el cuaderno.'
The teacher points to new words on the board: '___ la pizarra.'
Spanish class is over. The teacher says: '___ el bolígrafo y el cuaderno.'

objectives: Respond with the correct physical action to the three core command phrases (saquen el cuaderno, escuchen, levanten la mano)
Pick out a known object word inside a longer spoken command
Treat the plural -en command phrases as fixed classroom chunks, not forms to build or change
materialsNeeded: A notebook, pen, and ruler to mime with
A parent or teacher to call the commands aloud in random order
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Remind the child that a command tells you to do something now, like 'line up' at school.
2. Teach the three core phrases with a matching motion each: escuchen (hand to ear), levanten la mano (raise hand), saquen el cuaderno (mime taking out a notebook). Say each phrase, do the motion, have the child copy.
3. Add the extra commands (miren la pizarra, guarden el bolígrafo, abran/cierren el cuaderno), pointing out that the object word is one the child already knows.
4. Play the TPR game: call the phrases in a mixed order, speeding up, repeating slowly on any miss.
5. Stress that the child is only recognizing these phrases this week — how commands are actually built is a later lesson.
6. Do the cloze activity together.
7. Complete the worksheet.
8. Preview tomorrow's 'What's on my desk?' memory game.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use only the three core commands today, each locked to one motion, before adding any others
Ready for more: the child becomes the caller, giving you the commands to act out — a preview of Friday's student-teacher role

For the teaching adult: saquen, escuchen, and levanten are plural 'you all' commands (ustedes). The course teaches them as memorized phrases on purpose; the full command system, including the one-person forms, is scheduled for a later week, so there is no need to explain the -en ending now
This is a live listen-and-move activity, so it does not depend on the audio-recording gap noted elsewhere (open decision, expansion-plan-2026-09.md §12.9) — any adult can be the caller
teacherGuide.answerKey: Core commands: escuchen = listen; levanten la mano = raise your hand; saquen el cuaderno = take out your notebook. Extra commands: miren la pizarra = look at the board; guarden (el bolígrafo) = put away (your pen); abran / cierren el cuaderno = open / close your notebook. Cloze answers: 1. escuchen, 2. levanten, 3. saquen, 4. miren, 5. guarden. The action word comes first; the object word is one from Monday's list.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: This is the week's Interpretive Listening core (WA-WL-2015.1.2) and the exact Day 2 activity the scope-and-sequence names — classroom commands taught through Total Physical Response. Acting out a heard command is interpretive listening in its most observable form for a Novice learner, and anchoring each phrase to Monday's supply words lets the child parse a command by catching the object even before the action word is secure. Teaching the phrases as chunks keeps the cognitive load on comprehension, not on grammar the course sequences for later.

rows.problem: A teacher says 'saquen el cuaderno.' What do you do?
A teacher says 'escuchen.' What do you do?
A teacher says 'levanten la mano.' What do you do?

In the command 'guarden la regla,' which word is the object you already know, and what does it mean?
